narrative:
The model predicted a 70.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year ranking had a similar but slightly smaller effect in the same direction. These two performance measures outweighed everything else. Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the predicted risk of failure, but not enough to change the outcome.

Compared with students who were admitted, you ranked in the bottom decile for both first- and third-year performance, while admitted students averaged around the middle of their classes. Your LSAT score of 29 also sat well below the admitted average of 37, and your family income fell into the lower-middle bracket that is relatively uncommon among successful applicants.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Consider part-time study options if full-time work is limiting your preparation time. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to the current rejection. (218 words)
